You are outside a room with three switches, only one of which controls a single incandescent bulb inside the room. You may flip the switches as much as you like, but may only open the door and look inside the room once. How can you determine with certainty which switch controls the bulb?
choices: Turn switch 1 on for several minutes, then turn it off, turn switch 2 on, and enter: check both whether the bulb is lit and whether it feels warm

Premise 1: If it rains, the sidewalk gets wet. Premise 2: The sidewalk is wet. Many people conclude it must have rained. Is that conclusion logically valid?
choices: Yes, but only if it's currently cloudy
Yes — the sidewalk being wet proves it rained
No conclusion can ever be drawn from an if-then statement

questions.q: Across summer months, cities with higher ice cream sales also see more drowning deaths, and the two rise and fall together almost in lockstep. Does this mean eating ice cream increases your risk of drowning?
choices: Yes, but only for people who swim within an hour of eating
No, because correlation and causation are always unrelated
No — hot weather is a confounding variable that independently drives up both ice cream sales and swimming (and so drowning)
Yes, the correlation shows ice cream directly causes drowning

questions.q: Buses arrive at a certain stop following a Poisson process (perfectly memoryless and random) with an average of one bus every 10 minutes. If you walk up at a uniformly random moment, what is your expected waiting time for the next bus?
choices: It cannot be determined without knowing the exact schedule
10 minutes — memorylessness means your expected wait equals the full average interval, not half of it
5 minutes, half the average interval, since you arrive at a random point
